articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022, Issues General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. This action targets entities deemed to be involved in the theft or misappropriation of U.S. intellectual property.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses to provide guidance and authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. The specifics of the designated entities and the scope of the general licenses are detailed in the official announcement.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding American intellectual property and deterring foreign adversaries from engaging in economic espionage and theft.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License on October 16, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning certain transactions involving Venezuela.

Accompanying the amended General License, OFAC also published a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) to provide further clarity and guidance to stakeholders regarding the updated regulations and their implications.
These adjustments reflect OFAC's ongoing review and recalibration of its sanctions programs to address evolving policy considerations and humanitarian concerns in Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Iran and Cuba, Issues New and Amended General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran and a designation concerning Cuba on October 15, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs), to provide guidance on authorized transactions and compliance requirements.
These measures are part of the U.S. government's broader strategy to exert pressure on the Iranian and Cuban regimes and to prevent their access to the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action signifies a delisting of an individual or entity previously subject to U.S. sanctions.
Designation removals typically occur when the sanctioned party meets the criteria for delisting, such as a change in behavior or circumstances that led to the initial designation.
This removal indicates a potential shift in the U.S. government's assessment of the individual or entity's involvement in activities that previously warranted sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks supporting drug trafficking and terrorist organizations.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating global illicit finance and protecting the international financial system from abuse by criminal and terrorist groups.
These measures are part of a broader effort to degrade the operational capabilities of these networks and hold accountable those who facilitate their activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026, for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This settlement highlights OFAC's continued enforcement efforts against companies that fail to comply with U.S. sanctions.
In separate actions, OFAC also designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses, while simultaneously removing a Burma-related designation.
These diverse actions reflect OFAC's multi-faceted approach to sanctions implementation, encompassing enforcement, new designations, and delistings based on evolving geopolitical considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the extensive sanctions regime against Russia.

General Licenses are often issued to facilitate humanitarian aid, ensure the flow of certain essential goods, or to allow for the wind-down of specific operations, thereby mitigating unintended consequences of sanctions.
This issuance reflects OFAC's ongoing efforts to refine and adjust its Russia sanctions program in response to evolving circumstances and policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran-Related and Amended Russia-Related General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in activities supporting the Iranian regime. These actions aim to further restrict Iran's access to the international financial system.

Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These licenses provide specific authorizations for certain transactions, balancing sanctions pressure with humanitarian or other policy considerations.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's continued focus on both Iran and Russia, utilizing sanctions and targeted general licenses to achieve its foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designations removals and updates on October 5, 2026. These actions reflect ongoing adjustments to OFAC's sanctions lists, which can occur due to various factors such as changes in circumstances or successful delisting petitions.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert, providing important guidance and warnings to financial institutions and other stakeholders regarding potential sanctions risks associated with transactions involving Iran.
An amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) was also released, offering further clarification on specific aspects of the Iran sanctions program.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs.

The settlement addresses 475 apparent violations totaling approximately $14.8 million, which occurred between September 2021 and April 2025. These violations included 403 payments, amounting to $14.3 million, that were sent to or through 35 blocked banks.

OFAC's investigation revealed that an alert prioritization flaw and failures in watchlist updates allowed transactions involving three designated individuals and other blocked parties to proceed. The violations spanned various sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
